big: Rohan's policy has a ₹10 lakh cover. He picks a fancy hospital room. After the claim, he is surprised: the insurer paid much less than he expected, though nothing in the policy was excluded.

lines: My bill was covered but the insurer still paid less. How?
Four small clauses cause most of the surprises: co-payment, deductible, room rent limit and sub-limit.

alt: Two bars showing who pays under a 20% co-payment and under a room rent limit
caps: With a 20% co-payment, you pay a fifth of every claim.
If your room costs twice the limit, many policies cut related charges in the same proportion.
So a ₹1 lakh bill can leave you paying ₹50,000, though it was all covered.
Read these clauses before you buy, not after the claim.

intro: These also reduce what you receive.
rows: You bear the first part of a claim, say ₹50,000
A cap on one illness, such as ₹40,000 for cataract
note: A higher deductible lowers the premium, but only suits someone who can bear that part on their own.

q: A policy has a 20% co-payment. Meena's covered bill is ₹1.5 lakh. How much does the insurer pay?
opts: ₹1.5 lakh, since the whole bill is covered
₹1.2 lakh, since she bears 20%, which is ₹30,000
₹1.35 lakh, since the co-payment is only 10%
₹30,000, since the insurer pays the co-payment share
why: Co-payment means she shares each claim, so the insurer does not pay the whole bill.
Twenty percent of ₹1.5 lakh is ₹30,000, which she pays, and the insurer pays ₹1.2 lakh.
The co-payment is 20% here, not 10%, so the arithmetic is different.
The insurer pays the larger share. The co-payment is the part she pays herself.

q: A policy has a ₹50,000 deductible. Rohan's claim is ₹2 lakh. What does the insurer pay?
opts: ₹2 lakh, since the claim is within the cover
₹50,000, since that is what the policy sets
Nothing, since the claim is larger than the deductible
₹1.5 lakh, since he bears the first ₹50,000
why: A deductible is a part Rohan bears first, so the insurer does not pay it all.
₹50,000 is his own share of the bill, not what the insurer pays out.
A claim above the deductible is paid beyond it. It is not rejected.
He bears the first ₹50,000, and the insurer pays the remaining ₹1.5 lakh.

q: A policy caps room rent at ₹5,000 a day. Meena takes a ₹10,000 room. What is the risk?
opts: None, since the room is part of the covered bill
The insurer will refuse the whole claim for choosing the room
Related charges may be cut in proportion, so she pays much more
The sum insured will be reduced for the next year
why: A room limit can reduce other charges too, so the room choice does matter.
The claim is not refused for this. It is reduced in proportion.
Many policies cut related charges in proportion, so a costly room raises her share.
The sum insured for next year does not shrink because of a room choice.

q: Rohan has a cataract sub-limit of ₹40,000 and his bill is ₹60,000. What does he receive?
opts: ₹40,000, since the sub-limit caps this treatment
₹60,000, since the bill is within the sum insured
₹20,000, since the insurer pays only the extra amount
Nothing, since cataract is excluded by every policy
why: The sub-limit caps what is paid for this illness, so he gets ₹40,000 and pays ₹20,000.
A sub-limit overrides the sum insured for this treatment, so the full bill is not paid.
The insurer pays up to the limit, not only the amount above it.
Cataract is usually covered after a waiting period, within its sub-limit.

pts: Co-payment, deductible, room rent limit and sub-limit all cut what you receive.
A bill can be fully covered and still leave you paying a large share.
Read these four clauses before you buy.
